name: Stepanos of Taron
otherNames: Asoghik; Asolik and Asolnik in older spellings
Stephanos von Taron, in Heinrich Gelzer and August Burckhardt's German
Étienne de Tarôn, in Frédéric Macler's French
knownFor: An Armenian historian whose Universal History, written at the order of the catholicos Sargis, records the Bagratid kingdom of Armenia, its churches and its monasteries down to his own day. Its closing note gives the Armenian year 453, which Frédéric Macler reckons as 1004 to 1005.
dates: Finished his History in the Armenian year 453, which Frédéric Macler reckons as 1004 to 1005. Born after 927, by the Armenian editor Malkhasiants; Macler says he was at least about twenty by 967. Macler fits a manuscript notice of his death to 1021 (the scan reads 1091). J.-B. Emin, his Russian translator, had him die between 1041 and 1045, from a letter of Gregory Magistros; Malkhasiants found the age this gives him wholly unlikely. Marie-Félicité Brosset, a French translator of Armenian and Georgian chronicles, said no one knows when he died
place: Taron, the district his name comes from, as J.-B. Emin reads it; the monastery of Khladsor in Derjan, a district of Upper Armenia, where he spent a Lent; Ani, where the Bagratid kings ruled and where the catholicos Sargis moved his see in 992, Macler notes
role: Historian; writer of the Universal History at the order of the catholicos Sargis

keyWorks.title: Universal History
keyWorks.about: in three books, from the beginnings of the world to his own day. Book III runs from the start of the Bagratid dynasty in about 887, Macler says, with dates for almost every event. Held in Gelzer and Burckhardt's German (all three books, 1907) and in Macler's French (Book III, 1917)

traces: Macler counts nine manuscripts listed by Malkhasiants, who printed the Armenian text at St Petersburg in 1885, after Chahnazariants at Paris in 1859.
Translations followed into Russian by J.-B. Emin (1864), into French by Édouard Dulaurier (Books I and II, 1883) and Macler (Book III, 1917), and into German by Gelzer and Burckhardt (1907).

Marie-Félicité Brosset, in his French History of Georgia (1849), cites him again and again for dates and events. Jean-Baptiste Chabot, the editor of Michael the Syrian's Chronicle, points to his account of the synod of Manazkert.
remembered: Macler calls him the historian of the Bagratid kings who ruled at Ani, and the first Armenian writer whose dates can be trusted.
Gregory Magistros, an Armenian scholar, asks in a letter for a commentary on Jeremiah by Asolik, whom he calls a very old man (Macler's French).
C. F. Neumann, in 1830, called him "the learned Asolnik".

uncertain: His own life is thin. It rests on a few lines of his own and on modern editors who disagree. Macler warns that it is better to stay in near-ignorance than to fill the gap with bold guesses.

His name Asoghik. J.-B. Emin, his Russian translator, took it to mean he was skilled in church chant. Mélik David bey, whom Macler cites, read it as the little storyteller, which would rule out church chant.

His birth. Malkhasiants says the dates of his birth and death are unknown, and that he was born after 927. Emin made him about fifteen in 943. Macler, from Stepanos's own words about the old teachers, says he was at least about twenty by 967.

His death. Ghevond Alishan, an Armenian scholar, reported a manuscript at the Mekhitarist library in Venice that says the father of the monastery, Stephen, also Asoghik, died when the Persians took Kars. Macler notes that Alishan gives no account of the manuscript, and fits the only matching invasion to 1021. Emin, from a letter of Gregory Magistros, had him alive until 1041 to 1045 and dying at about 117 or 129; Malkhasiants found that age wholly unlikely, and Macler answers that Gregory wrote for years after, so one could as well say Stepanos was alive then. Brosset, in 1876, said no one knows when he died.
His burial. Armenian tradition shows his tomb at Mush, in the cemetery of the monastery of the Holy Apostles. Macler says the tradition needs a very close look.

His office. He says he wrote amid the sacred duties Sargis gave him, without naming them. Garegin Zarbhanalean, in a history of Armenian literature (1897), says he studied at Ani and was ordained a priest; Macler says that does little to settle the question. Alishan cites a list that makes Asolik the vardapet and Stephen of Taron the historian two men, and says he was thought to be a cantor from Taron (the scan is garbled at this word); Macler doubts the list.

When the History ends. One line has Senekerim reign twenty years, which would reach 1023 or 1024. Malkhasiants reads one year, which keeps the History ending in 1004 or 1005. Brosset saw at least two later insertions in Book III. Michael Chamich's History of Armenia, in Johannes Avdall's English of 1827, has it run to the year 1000. F. C. Conybeare placed the writing between 991 and 1019, as Macler quotes him (the scan of Conybeare's page reads 19190).

Which Anania ordered the second baptism. Stepanos names Anania of Narek among the teachers, and says the ruling came at the order of the lord Anania. Macler takes that Anania to be the catholicos, Anania of Mokq.
Gregory Magistros's letter is undated, Macler notes, and no commentary on Jeremiah by Stepanos survives.
